A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on defining and measuring disentanglement under dependent factors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions and a changed title.

before.justification: v1 reports original cosine-dependence and conditionally colored-MNIST experiments in Sections 5–6, plus nuisance experiments in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original dependence and nuisance experiments, plus evaluations of learned representations on DSprites, MPI3D, and Shapes3D in Sections 5–6.

M1.justification: v1 Section 4 and Appendix B compute scores using regressors and noise-normalized prediction errors. v2 Sections 4.3–4.4 replace these with normalized mutual-information ratios estimated through discretization, and replace weighted minimality aggregation with an unweighted average. Minimality and sufficiency already existed in v1; their computation changes substantially.

E1.justification: The conditionally colored-MNIST evaluation is removed and replaced by DSprites, MPI3D, and Shapes3D experiments. v2 also evaluates pairwise-dependence and shared-confounder scenarios on these datasets. Synthetic dependence and nuisance coverage remains, although its construction changes.

E2.justification: The nuisance comparison expands from the authors' modularity and minimality variants in v1 Appendix C to include FactorVAE, MIG, SAP, Modularity, Disentanglement, and Completeness in v2 Figure 3. Explicitness Score and Informativeness, evaluated in v1 Tables 4 and 8, disappear from the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: The fixed three-factor continuous cosine cases become four-factor categorical experiments with dependence and mixing parameter sweeps. The new neural evaluation uses six architectures crossed with six losses per dataset, and rank correlations with single-dimension prediction accuracy using 1000 training samples and with IRS. These are new evaluation designs, not documented reruns of the earlier settings.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the fixed dependence and nuisance cases with systematic sensitivity curves and adds analyses connecting metric scores to prediction accuracy and interventional robustness across dependence regimes. The colored-MNIST controlled-generation demonstration and the appendix's per-variable modularity-versus-minimality analysis are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars for its own results. v2 introduces rank correlations as evaluation outcomes without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The fixed cosine, colored-MNIST, and per-variable nuisance results are replaced by the curves and correlation results in v2 Figures 2–5. New findings include strong, comparatively stable accuracy correlations for Sufficiency and IRS correlations for Minimality across three datasets. These results concern changed methods and settings, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: v2 Theorem 1 strengthens v1 Propositions 2–3 from one-way implications into an equivalence and adds a reverse-direction argument in Appendix A. Section 4.3 also introduces formal normalized mutual-information score definitions. The earlier sufficiency equivalence is largely retained as Theorem 2 under renamed properties.

C1.justification: v2 makes four properties and their claimed equivalence to minimality and sufficiency central contributions, strengthening v1's sufficient-condition guarantee. Minimality, sufficiency, and nuisance invariance move from supporting material into the principal formulation. The conclusion additionally claims reliable relationships with downstream performance under dependence.

C2.justification: v2 develops information-fraction interpretations, explains why greater factor dependence can increase scores for mixed representations, and connects sufficiency and minimality to prediction and robustness respectively. Section 6 explicitly acknowledges unavailable ground-truth disentanglement for learned representations. The earlier discussion of regressor capacity and its influence on explicitness scores is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project code link, specifies 15-bin representation discretization, and supplies training hyperparameters and detailed architecture tables in Appendices B–C. These replace v1 Appendix D's colored-MNIST conditional-prior, architecture, and training details alongside the changed experiments.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the broad survey of representation-learning methods with focused dependent-factor and causal research positioning, adding works including Träuble et al. (2021), Roth et al. (2022), Ahuja et al. (2023), and von Kügelgen et al. (2024). It expands information-bottleneck positioning and explicitly claims the first formal definition through minimal sufficient representations.

P1.justification: The title, author list, and much of the prose change. The narrative is reorganized around four properties, dedicated minimality/sufficiency sections, and separate toy and neural evaluations. Related work and appendices are extensively restructured, beyond changes attributable solely to added experiments.

P2.justification: v1's algorithm blocks, numerical experiment tables, and generated-MNIST image grid are replaced by a conceptual diagram, sensitivity plots, and multi-panel correlation charts. v2 also introduces extensive appendix architecture tables and substantially changes typography and page layout.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support beyond v1's single tailored MNIST model through broader model comparisons and downstream validation, while adding useful implementation documentation. However, its newly central Theorem 1 equivalence is unsupported: Appendix A's converse requires joint conditional independence from other factors and nuisances, which the separately stated independence conditions do not establish. This substantive theoretical defect accompanies substantial empirical and documentation gains, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
